Dartmouth College is a research institution designated by the [Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education](/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") as having "very high research activity".[[68]](#cite_note-68) In 2019, Dartmouth College was elected to the [Association of American Universities](/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities") (AAU), an organization of 69 research universities.[[69]](#cite_note-69)

Faculty members have been at the forefront of such major academic developments as the [Dartmouth Workshop](/wiki/Dartmouth_Workshop "Dartmouth Workshop"), the [Dartmouth Time-Sharing System](/wiki/Dartmouth_Time-Sharing_System "Dartmouth Time-Sharing System"), [Dartmouth BASIC](/wiki/Dartmouth_BASIC "Dartmouth BASIC"), and [Dartmouth ALGOL 30](/wiki/Dartmouth_ALGOL_30 "Dartmouth ALGOL 30"). In 2005, sponsored project awards to Dartmouth faculty research amounted to $169 million.[[70]](#cite_note-Academics_&_Research-70)

In 2017, [Eric Fossum](/wiki/Eric_Fossum "Eric Fossum"), a professor of engineering at Dartmouth College, was awarded the [Queen Elizabeth Prize](/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_Prize "Queen Elizabeth Prize") for his work on imaging sensor technology.[[71]](#cite_note-71) The [Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine](/wiki/Pfizer%E2%80%93BioNTech_COVID-19_vaccine "Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine"), which was approved in 2021, was based on findings that originated in a science lab at the college.[[72]](#cite_note-72) In 2024, researchers at Dartmouth received a $31.3 million grant from the federal government to further their study of prostate cancer.[[73]](#cite_note-73) In 2025, Dartmouth received approximately $97 million worth of funding from the [National Institutes of Health](/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health").[[74]](#cite_note-74)

War of the Third Coalition :: Battle of Austerlitz :: French plans and dispositions :: chunk_0021
Days before any actual fighting, Napoleon had given an impression to the Allies that his army was in a weak state and that he desired a negotiated peace.[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcLynn1997342-31) In reality, he was hoping that they would attack, and to encourage them on this mission he deliberately weakened his right flank.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrooks2000109-32) On 28 November, Napoleon met with his marshals at Imperial Headquarters and they informed him of their qualms and fears about the upcoming battle, even suggesting a retreat, but he shrugged off their complaints and went to work.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFisherFremont-Barnes200448-33) Napoleon's plan envisioned that the Allies would throw so many troops to envelop his right flank that their centre would be severely weakened. He then counted on a massive French thrust, to be conducted by 16,000 troops of [Soult](/wiki/Nicolas_Jean_de_Dieu_Soult "Nicolas Jean de Dieu Soult")'s IV Corps, through the centre to cripple the Allied army. Meanwhile, to support his weak right flank, Napoleon ordered Davout's [III Corps](/wiki/III_Corps_(Grande_Arm%C3%A9e) "III Corps (Grande Armée)") to force march all the way from Vienna and join General Legrand's men, who held the extreme southern flank that would bear the heavy part of the Allied attack. Davout's soldiers had 48 hours to March 110 km (68 mi). Their arrival would be extremely crucial in determining the success or failure of the French plan. The [Imperial Guard](/wiki/French_Imperial_Guard "French Imperial Guard") and [Bernadotte](/wiki/Charles_XIV_John_of_Sweden "Charles XIV John of Sweden")'s I Corps were held in reserve while the V Corps under [Lannes](/wiki/Jean_Lannes "Jean Lannes") guarded the northern sector of the battle.

The new kingdom was reliant on limited agriculture and pilgrimage revenues.[[109]](#cite_note-114) [In 1938, vast reserves of oil were discovered](/wiki/Dammam_No._7 "Dammam No. 7") in the Al-Ahsa region along the coast of the Persian Gulf, and full-scale development of the oil fields began in 1941 under the US-controlled [Aramco (Arabian American Oil Company)](/wiki/Saudi_Aramco "Saudi Aramco"). Oil provided Saudi Arabia with economic prosperity and substantial political leverage internationally.[[78]](#cite_note-Britannica_history-83) Cultural life rapidly developed, primarily in the Hejaz, which was the centre for newspapers and radio.
